summary: Specifies a way to carry long addresses in the HOST-PORT part of FTP's data port command, so FTP can work with next-generation IP alternatives and perhaps other transports besides TCP. It is experimental. It was replaced by RFC 1639.

eli5.summary: The old FTP form had small boxes for an address. This memo makes room for longer addresses so it can work with bigger future networks.

questions: ftp operation over big address records
subtitle: FTP commands to handle longer addresses from next-generation IP protocols.

tldr.problem: The original FTP PORT command carries a 32-bit IP address and 16-bit port number in a fixed format, but next-generation IP protocols will use much longer addresses, and other transports may use longer port numbers too.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1545 defines two new commands: LPRT (Long PORT) allows the client to specify address family, variable-length host address, and variable-length port number. LPSV (Long Passive) is the passive-mode equivalent. The address family field lets clients request any IP version number or future protocol.
tldr.outcome: This experimental protocol was a bridge toward IPv6, but IPv6 eventually became standardized and FTP was updated with its own IPv6 extensions. RFC 1639 replaced it.

today: RFC 1545 is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 1639. IPv6 was eventually standardized and FTP specifications were updated to handle it.

sections.title: The PORT Command Problem
sections.content: The classic FTP PORT command lets a client tell the server where to send data: it concatenates a 32-bit IP host address and a 16-bit TCP port into six decimal numbers separated by commas (e.g., PORT 128,3,4,5,17,1 for address 128.3.4.5 port 4353). This works fine for IPv4 and TCP ports, but next-generation IP protocols (IPNG) will use much longer addresses, and some non-TCP transports may use longer port numbers. FTP needed a new command to handle variable-length addresses.
sections.eli5: The old FTP address format was designed for small addresses. As computer networks grew, bigger addresses were needed.

sections.title: The LPRT and LPSV Commands
sections.content: RFC 1545 defines the LPRT (Long PORT) command with the syntax LPRT af,hal,h1,h2,...,pal,p1,p2,.... The af field specifies an address family (an IP version number or protocol identifier), hal and the host bytes specify the host address, pal and the port bytes specify the transport address. The LPSV (Long Passive) command lets the server respond with the same structure when the client requests passive mode. The RFC also reserves error code 521 to indicate that the server does not support the requested address family.
sections.eli5: LPRT and LPSV are FTP commands that work like PORT and PASV but can handle addresses of any size. The server can say whether it supports the address type you are asking for.

sections.title: Design for Flexibility
sections.content: The mechanism is intentionally flexible. The address family argument allows support for any IPNG alternative, and the explicit length fields for both address and port let FTP work over multiple transport protocols at once. Some transport protocols (such as TP/IX) already support port selectors longer than 16 bits, and the design anticipates even multi-protocol environments like Appletalk, IPX, and OSI networks.
sections.eli5: The design is open-ended so that as new networks and protocols appear, FTP can work with them all without needing to reinvent the command again.
